doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Father in Vietnam, leaving business school for music, and playing with Chet Baker
summary: His father went to Vietnam; Stanford MBA classmates put him off, so he turned to music, including brief Monday gigs with Chet Baker.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: into helicopters. So he became a commander. Because he was a Colonel when he retired. But pop was a chopper commander so when he was transferred at the end of my freshman year, the summer that I went back to Germany between my freshman and sophomore years, he got orders to Vietnam and so he was the first group of the big buildup of choppers that they started to ship over to Vietnam for the war. So we picked up the summer of ’65 and went back to the Peninsula. Of course I was going to school, I had to finish my freshman year already in Claremont and so I was just coming back to California anyhow. But now the whole family went back and then pop went on to Vietnam. But he wound up there — he was there for about 15 months I guess and got a Purple Heart and all that sort of stuff. But he was really gung ho trying to get me to go, because I was in ROTC and all that sort of stuff. But I couldn’t see going. And there were a lot of other circumstances. I wound up not going. But the point was that in B school, here I’ve got these pilots coming back and they’re all like, “Oh yeah we’re really — we’re Vietnam veterans” and most of these guys were in carriers, took off every day. By that time, 1970, there was hardly any SAMS — you know surface-to-air missiles coming up at ‘em. And there were no MIGS anymore. They shot all the North Vietnamese MIGS down. I mean the early sixties, when my father was there, ’65, ’66, ’67, that’s when those guys got creamed. That’s when McCain wound up getting shot down and all these guys were shot down and POWs and all. But after, from 1969 on, there’s no resistance in the skies. Americans did whatever they wanted to do. So anyway, to make a long story short, these guys are coming back all cocky and all this kind of — I said wait a minute. If I get this MBA and go off in that direction I’m going wind up — these are my significant others, this is my good old boy network. I’ve got to call up that — can I say asshole — I’m going to have to call that asshole and say okay look, I’ve got a deal here with my company and blah blah blah, or I’m going to sit on a board of directors across from them and be saying oh I think we need to do this. Man, you were an asshole at Stanford and you’re still an asshole. Why do I have to listen to this bullshit. This is not right for what we need to do with this board of directors up here. So I said to myself well if that’s the way I feel I need to think about what I really want to do with my life. And of course I had been playing all the time, playing gigs and bar mitzvahs and weddings and big bands and even doing jazz gigs. I mean I was up playing with different jazz musicians both locally and occasionally do something with somebody that’s more known. I was even playing for instance Monday nights with Chet Baker. You know Chet Baker got out of prison and his mother was living up in Milpitas, just north of San Jose. And I used to go over to Chet’s mother’s house and we would rehearse. We had this Monday night gig in a pizza parlor in San Jose. And later Chet moved up to San Francisco and so he had me working. I only lasted a couple of Mondays, or I forget how often he was — yeah it was every week in

San Francisco and I only lasted there for about two or three weeks because by that time I was already a musician up there and it was so ridiculous because Chet was really trying to just score, trying to get some stuff together. So sometimes we wouldn’t even get paid. So I mean it was just some silly stuff. So I said later for this. But in San Jose, earlier, I did things like that. So I said to myself you know that’s really something that I really enjoy doing is playing the music. And of course I’d been learning tunes and writing things, and I’d learned how to play piano and had this record collection that kept getting bigger and bigger and bigger, because I’d been collecting records since I was about nine, ten years old and just enjoying the music. Like I told everybody in the clinic, I was a listener long before I was a performer. And I’ve chosen never to lose my listening chops. Never.
